What goes into the soundtrack that isn't music or dialogue, and how we're doing it for "The Last Tram to Auchenshuggle". The cutting side, picture and sound together, is in [[Editing rhythm]].

## Where the term comes from

Walter Murch got the credit "Sound Designer" on "Apocalypse Now" (1979), the first time anybody had it. Ben Burtt did the "Star Wars" sounds the same decade: the lightsaber is a projector motor hum plus a buzz from a broken TV set. Every sound designer since has a story like that.

## Layers

- Dialogue, recorded on set or redone (ADR).
- Foley: footsteps, cloth, props, done in a room to picture.
- Effects: doors, trams, rain.
- Ambience and room tone: 30 seconds of "silence" from every location, so the edit doesn't drop to dead air between lines.
- Music last.

## Recording the tram

Riverside Museum let us record in the 1938 Coronation tram (car 1282) on 9 July 2025, 8am before opening. Zoom H5 at 48 kHz/24-bit, Rode NTG2 shotgun on a boom. Got: doors, the bell, the controller handle clicking through notches, seat springs, and 4 minutes of room tone. The tram can't move, so the running sound is a recording of a Blackpool tram, licensed from a library for £18 (ref SFXL-40291).

## Low end and fear

Horror relies on frequencies you feel more than hear. Infrasound under 20 Hz was used in "Irréversible" (2002) to make people sick on purpose. At the club horror night the sub from my flat added more dread than the film's score, see [[Horror movie night]].

## Our ending

The script ends with the tram driving past the terminus into the dark. We can't film that, so the plan: hold on Margaret's face, take the room tone away, then bring in the motor rising and the bell once, far off. Sound does the moving. Pad underneath from the Minilogue, see [[Synth patch notes]], and mixed in the box room, see [[Mixing vocals]] for how the reverb sits.
